extra.message: User-supplied search term from request.args.get('search') (line 126) is interpolated directly into an SQL string via f-string at line 137: s_query = f"SELECT filename FROM files WHERE user_id = {user_id} AND filename LIKE '%{search_query}%'" and executed at line 138 without parameterization. An attacker can break out of the LIKE '%...%' literal (e.g. ' OR 1=1 --) to read or modify arbitrary database data, including all users' password hashes.

The /upload endpoint saves files using the client-supplied filename without sanitization: filename = file.filename (line 262), filepath = os.path.join(UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename) (line 263), file.save(filepath) (line 264). Werkzeug's secure_filename is never applied, so a crafted multipart filename such as '../../server/config.py' allows writing arbitrary files anywhere the process can write (arbitrary file overwrite, e.g. overwriting application code or templates). Additionally there is no validation of file extension or content, permitting upload of dangerous file types (CWE-434).

extra.message: The unauthenticated POST /api/v1/update_picture endpoint fetches a user-supplied URL with requests.get(picture_url) (line 254) with no URL allowlist, scheme, or host validation. An attacker can force the server to issue requests to internal-only resources (e.g. cloud metadata endpoints such as http://169.254.169.254/, localhost services, or internal network hosts). The endpoint also updates the profile picture of an arbitrary 'username' from the request body without any authentication.

The @token_required authentication decorator is commented out (lines 152-153) on GET /api/v1/profile. The endpoint returns username, email, country, role, permissions, and team for any user based solely on the user-supplied user_id query parameter, with no authentication or authorization. Any unauthenticated attacker can enumerate user_id values and harvest every user's personal and authorization data (sensitive data exposure / broken object level authorization).

The handler (line 223) deletes any user account without verifying the caller's identity or privileges (no admin check). extra.message: The POST /update_profile endpoint accepts 'role' and 'permissions' directly from request.form (lines 187-196) and writes them to the users table (line 234) without any authorization check. Any authenticated user can POST role=admin&permissions=all to elevate themselves to administrator (mass assignment privilege escalation). The corresponding inputs are merely commented out in client/templates/edit_profile.html (lines 39-43), which does not prevent a crafted request from setting these fields.

extra.message: The Flask SECRET_KEY is hardcoded as "just_another_secret". It is used to sign Flask session cookies and the JWTs issued by POST /api/v1/login and validated by @token_required (server/api/v1/api_v1.py lines 94 and 133). Anyone with access to this public source can forge valid session cookies and admin JWT tokens, achieving complete authentication bypass.

The dashboard template renders the search term with the Jinja2 'safe' filter: value="{{ search_query | safe }}", which disables HTML autoescaping. search_query originates from request.args.get('search') in the /dashboard route (server/routes.py:126) and is passed to render_template (server/routes.py:143). An attacker can craft a link such as /dashboard?search="><script>...</script> to execute arbitrary JavaScript in a victim's browser; combined with SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=False this enables session cookie theft and account hijacking.

extra.message: The profile template renders the user-controlled 'country' field with the 'safe' filter: {{ user.country | safe }}, disabling Jinja2 autoescaping. The country value is set by the user via the /update_profile form (server/routes.py:186) and stored in the database before being rendered on the profile page — a stored/persistent XSS allowing script execution in the browser of anyone viewing the profile.

extra.message: Passwords are hashed with unsalted MD5: custom_hash() returns hashlib.md5(password.encode()).hexdigest() (line 403). It is used for password storage at signup (line 93) and verification at login (line 50). MD5 is cryptographically broken and these hashes are trivially reversed using rainbow tables or GPU brute-force, so any database disclosure reveals every user's password. A salted slow KDF (bcrypt/scrypt/argon2) is required.

cwe: CWE-327: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
CWE-916: Use of Password Hash With Insufficient Computational Effort

extra.message: DEBUG = True is applied via app.run(debug=debug_mode) in run.py (line 10), enabling the Werkzeug interactive debugger. On any unhandled exception the debugger console permits execution of arbitrary Python code on the server (remote code execution); the debugger PIN can be leaked through the debug output or brute-forced. Debug mode must never be enabled in production.

SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY = False (applied to the app in run.py line 9) makes the session cookie readable by JavaScript. Combined with the reflected XSS in dashboard.html and stored XSS in profile.html, this allows an attacker to steal the session cookie and hijack the victim's authenticated session.

The /uploads/profile_pictures/<filename> route serves profile pictures with send_from_directory(PROFILE_PICTURES_UPLOAD_FOLDER, filename) and no authentication or ownership check, unlike /uploads/<filename> and /download/<filename> which verify the session and that the file belongs to the requesting user. Any unauthenticated user can enumerate and download all users' uploaded profile pictures.

cwe: CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function

extra.message: Hardcoded plaintext passwords ('super-secret', 'password123', 'my-secret', 'password', 'password1') for eight named accounts are inserted into the application database by this seeding script, including the admin account john_doe with password 'super-secret' and full permissions. Anyone with repository access knows valid credentials for these accounts.

The exception handler in POST /api/v1/update_picture returns {'message': str(e)}, 500 to the client, exposing internal error details. For requests.get() failures this can reveal internal hostnames, IP addresses, and network topology, turning the SSRF in this endpoint into a semi-blind primitive that leaks whether internal hosts/ports are reachable.

cwe: CWE-209: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information

extra.message: Flask's MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH is never configured and file.save(filepath) writes the entire uploaded request body to disk with no size limit. An authenticated user can repeatedly upload arbitrarily large files to exhaust disk space and deny service to all users of the application.

The session cookie is explicitly configured in run.py (name and HttpOnly flag), but SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is never set anywhere, so Flask's default (False) applies and the session cookie is transmitted over unencrypted HTTP. A network attacker positioned between the client and server can intercept the session cookie and hijack the session.
